title: Palindrome Linked List
directAnswer: For O(1) space: find the middle with fast/slow pointers, reverse the second half in place, then walk the first half and the reversed second half forward comparing values node-by-node. If every pair matches it's a palindrome. The cheap-and-clear alternative is to copy all values into an array and use two-pointer comparison — O(n) time but O(n) space. Optionally restore the reversed half before returning to leave the input untouched.

remember.pattern: Fast/slow midpoint + reverse second half + two-pointer compare
remember.formula:
# 1. find middle
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
# 2. reverse from slow
prev = None
while slow:
    nxt = slow.next; slow.next = prev; prev = slow; slow = nxt
# 3. compare halves
left, right = head, prev
while right:
    if left.val != right.val: return False
    left = left.next; right = right.next
return True
rules: Find the middle with **fast/slow**, then reverse from `slow` to the end — you compare the first half against the reversed second half.
Stop the comparison when the **second-half (right) pointer** hits null; the reversed half is the shorter/equal one, so it's the safe loop guard.
An **odd-length** list has a lone middle node that pairs with itself — the right-half walk naturally stops before forcing it to match anything.
Reversing **mutates the input**. If the caller must see the original list, reverse the second half **back** before returning.
Use `fast and fast.next` for the midpoint so `fast.next.next` never dereferences null.
The array approach is **O(n) space** but trivially correct — name it as the fallback, then offer the O(1) reverse-half method as the upgrade.
whenToUse: Check symmetry of a singly linked list with O(1) extra space
Any problem needing the reversed second half compared against the first (Reorder List shares the split+reverse)
Demonstrating composition of two primitives: midpoint-finding and in-place reversal
When recursion depth (O(n) stack) or an array copy (O(n) space) is unacceptable
antiSignals: Mutating the input is forbidden and you can't restore it → copy values to an array instead
It's a doubly linked list → walk inward from both ends, no reversal needed
Values are huge objects, not cheap ints → comparison cost may dominate; reconsider copying
remember.takeaway: Palindrome Linked List is the textbook 'compose two primitives' problem: fast/slow to split, three-pointer flip to reverse, then a linear compare. If you've mastered Middle of the Linked List and Reverse Linked List, this is just gluing them together — and that composition mindset is exactly what interviewers reward.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can compose the midpoint and reversal primitives into an O(1)-space solution, rather than defaulting to the O(n)-space array copy — and whether you handle odd lengths and (ideally) restore the list.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing against the wrong length (looping until the first-half pointer ends rather than the reversed second half), or mishandling the odd-length middle node so the comparison is off by one.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Offer the simple array solution first to anchor correctness, then upgrade to the O(1)-space reverse-half method, explicitly handle the odd middle, and mention restoring the list to leave the input pristine.

problemStatement:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list, return `true` if it is a *palindrome* or `false` otherwise.

A list is a palindrome when the sequence of node values reads the same forwards and backwards.

**Follow-up:** Could you do it in `O(n)` time and `O(1)` extra space?
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [1, 10⁵]
A single node and an empty list are considered palindromes
understanding: We compare the value sequence against its reverse. The trivial check copies values to an array and uses two pointers from both ends. The interview-grade follow-up demands O(1) space: split the list at its middle, reverse the second half in place, and walk both halves inward-to-outward comparing values. Only the values matter — node identity doesn't — but because we mutate pointers to achieve O(1) space, leaving the list intact is a thoughtful extra.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Am I allowed to modify the list, or must it stay intact?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The O(1)-space method reverses the second half in place. If the list must stay intact, I'll reverse that half back before returning — same complexity, just one extra pass.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is O(n) space acceptable, or do you want the O(1)-space follow-up?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll mention the O(n)-space array copy for clarity, then implement the O(1)-space reverse-half version since that's the follow-up interviewers want.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How should I treat empty or single-node lists?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both are palindromes — return true. The algorithm handles them naturally: the comparison loop simply doesn't run, or runs zero useful times.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the values simple comparables?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, integers here. I compare with ==; for richer payloads I'd compare with the appropriate equality.

examples.explanation: Even length. Middle splits into [1, 2] and [2, 1]; reversing the second gives [1, 2], which matches the first half.
Odd length. Middle node 3 pairs with itself; first half [1, 2] vs reversed back half [1, 2] match.
Reversed second half [2] compared to first [1] — 1 ≠ 2, not a palindrome.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach

approaches.name: Copy to Array — Two-Pointer Compare
approaches.whenToMention: State this first as the obviously-correct baseline. It's the safe answer when mutation is forbidden or O(n) space is fine.
hints: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. If the values were in an array, how would you check that in one pass?
Copy every node's value into an array, then use two pointers — one at each end — moving inward and comparing.
If any left/right pair differs, return false; if the pointers cross without a mismatch, return true. O(n) time but O(n) space for the array.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to copy n values into an array (O(n) time, O(n) space), then at most n/2 comparisons walking the two pointers inward (O(n) time). Total O(n) time, O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Flatten the list into an array of values, then run the standard array-palindrome check with two pointers converging from the ends.

**Why this is the natural first answer.** Palindrome checking is trivial on a structure with random access: compare index `i` with index `n-1-i` for `i` up to the middle. A singly linked list lacks random access and can't be walked backwards, so the simplest fix is to *give* ourselves random access by copying the values into an array. Now the textbook two-pointer compare applies directly.

**Why we compare values, not nodes.** A palindrome is about the *sequence of values*, so once the values are in the array the original nodes are irrelevant. This also sidesteps any concern about mutating the list — we never touch the links.

**Why two pointers from the ends.** Moving `left` up from `0` and `right` down from `n-1`, comparing as we go, checks the i-th symmetric pair in O(1) each. The moment a pair disagrees we can short-circuit to `false`; if they meet or cross, every symmetric pair matched and it's a palindrome.

**Why we ultimately prefer the O(1)-space method.** This solution is correct and easy to get right under pressure, which is why it's worth stating. But it uses O(n) auxiliary space, and the explicit follow-up asks for O(1). So we present this for clarity and then upgrade — showing the interviewer both that we can ship something correct fast and that we can optimise when pushed.
approaches.insight: Copying to an array is the universal 'I can't index this structure, so I'll borrow indexing' move. It instantly reduces a linked-list problem to its array form — a great first answer that also makes the O(1)-space optimisation easy to motivate by contrast.

approaches.name: Reverse Second Half — O(1) Space (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The follow-up answer. Frame it as 'compose three primitives: find middle, reverse the back half, compare the halves'.
hints: A palindrome means the first half equals the reversed second half. You already know how to find the middle and how to reverse a list — can you combine them?
Step 1: fast/slow pointers to reach the middle. Step 2: reverse the list from the middle to the end. Step 3: walk the first half and the reversed second half together, comparing values.

Loop the comparison while the reversed (second-half) pointer is non-null — it's the shorter or equal side, so an odd middle node is skipped harmlessly. Optionally reverse the second half back to restore the input.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Finding the middle is one pass (O(n)). Reversing the second half touches n/2 nodes (O(n)). Comparing walks n/2 pairs (O(n)). All sequential, no extra data structure → O(n) time, O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
We exploit a clean definition: a list is a palindrome exactly when its first half equals its second half read backwards. Rather than copy anything, we physically reverse the back half so it can be read 'backwards' by walking forward, then compare the two halves in lockstep.

**Step 1 — split with fast/slow.** Run the tortoise-and-hare midpoint finder. When `fast` falls off the end, `slow` sits at the start of the second half (for even lengths) or on the middle node (for odd lengths). This is the same primitive as Middle of the Linked List, reused verbatim — a sign you've decomposed the problem well.

**Step 2 — reverse from slow.** Apply the standard `prev/curr/next` three-pointer flip starting at `slow`. After this, `prev` is the head of the reversed second half — i.e. the original last node. The first half still runs forward from `head`. Crucially, for odd lengths the lone middle node ends up as the tail of *both* conceptual halves, and it simply pairs with itself, so it never causes a mismatch.

**Step 3 — compare inward-to-outward.** Walk `left` from `head` and `right` from `prev` simultaneously, comparing `left.val == right.val`. **Why we stop when `right` hits null:** the reversed second half is the shorter-or-equal side (it never exceeds half the list), so using it as the loop guard checks every meaningful pair without overrunning. For odd lengths, `right` reaches null exactly when the unmatched middle would come up, so we never wrongly compare it. If any pair differs we return `false`; surviving the loop means it's a palindrome.

**Optional step 4 — restore.** Because we mutated the back half, the caller's list is now altered. Reversing the second half *again* puts every pointer back, leaving the input pristine at the cost of one more O(n) pass and no extra space. Mentioning this unprompted signals senior-level care about side effects.
approaches.insight: This is two well-known primitives bolted together: midpoint via fast/slow and in-place reversal via prev/curr/next. The meta-skill is recognising that a hard-looking problem is really 'find middle' + 'reverse' + 'compare' — decomposition beats cleverness, and the same split+reverse opens Reorder List too.

code.python:
def isPalindrome(self, head: ListNode) -> bool:
    if not head or not head.next:
        return True
    # 1. find middle
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    # 2. reverse from slow to the end
    prev, curr = None, slow
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    # 3. compare first half with reversed second half
    left, right = head, prev
    ok = True
    while right:
        if left.val != right.val:
            ok = False
            break
        left = left.next
        right = right.next
    # 4. (optional) restore the second half
    prev2, cur2 = None, prev
    while cur2:
        nxt = cur2.next
        cur2.next = prev2
        prev2 = cur2
        cur2 = nxt
    return ok

pitfalls: Looping the comparison while `left != null` instead of `right != null` — overruns on the odd middle and can misread.
Forgetting that the reverse mutates the input; if the list must stay intact, restore it.
Skipping the empty/single-node short-circuit and then dereferencing null in the midpoint loop.
Reversing from head.next or the wrong node instead of slow — misaligns the halves.

commonMistakes: Looping the comparison against the first-half length instead of the reversed second half — off-by-one on odd lengths.
Leaving the list mutated when the caller expects it intact (forgetting to restore).
Defaulting to the O(n)-space array when the follow-up explicitly asks for O(1).
Mishandling the odd middle node so it's wrongly forced to match a neighbour.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong comparison loop guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The reversed second half is the shorter-or-equal side. Guarding on the first-half pointer (left) instead of right makes the loop run one step too long on odd lengths, dereferencing past the intended pairs.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
left, right = head, prev
while left:            # first half is longer on odd lengths
    if left.val != right.val:
        return False
    left = left.next
    right = right.next  # right becomes None, then .val crashes
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
left, right = head, prev
while right:           # reversed half is the safe, shorter guard
    if left.val != right.val:
        return False
    left = left.next
    right = right.next

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not restoring a mutated list
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The O(1)-space method reverses the back half in place. If the caller still needs the original list (or tests it afterward), leaving it reversed is a silent corruption bug.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
# ... compare halves ...
return ok   # list's second half is left reversed
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# ... compare halves ...
prev2, cur2 = None, prev
while cur2:
    nxt = cur2.next
    cur2.next = prev2
    prev2 = cur2
    cur2 = nxt
return ok   # original order restored

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Crashing the midpoint loop on tiny lists
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without an empty/single-node guard, the same fast.next.next dereference risk applies; and for a clean structure, short-circuiting trivial palindromes is clearer.

The split-then-reverse setup is shared with Reorder List, the reversal subroutine is Reverse Linked List, and the midpoint step is Middle of the Linked List. Recognise it whenever you must compare a list against its own reverse without extra space.
